name: Kurseong
tagline: The orchid town where the toy train runs through the bazaar
meta_description: Kurseong on a budget: Netaji's house at Giddapahar, Eagle's Crag, the toy train bazaar, Makaibari, shared jeep fares, homestay prices and best months.
summary: Kurseong is a hill town of about 1,480 m, 32 km below Darjeeling and 1.5–2 hours from Siliguri. It has Netaji's house at Giddapahar, the toy train running through its bazaar, old schools at Dow Hill and tea gardens all round. Budget rooms start around ₹1,200; shared jeeps from Siliguri cost ₹150–200.

local_story.title: Kharsang, the orchid town that held Netaji
paras: Ask anyone in Kurseong what the name means and you will hear the same answer: it comes from the Lepcha word Kharsang, usually translated as 'land of the white orchid'. The orchid people point to is Coelogyne cristata, a white flower that hangs from mossy trees on these slopes in late winter. Another explanation ties the name to a local cane. The land itself passed from Sikkim to Nepal around 1780, back to Sikkim under the Treaty of Titalia in 1817, and into British hands with the Darjeeling tract. Kurseong became a municipality in 1879.

In 1922 the lawyer Sarat Chandra Bose bought a house on Giddapahar, the hill above the town, as a family retreat. His younger brother Subhas came here several times, and in 1936, after returning from Europe, he was held at the house under British house arrest. From this house he wrote political letters and letters to Emilie Schenkl in Austria. The Bose family kept it until the 1990s; it is now the Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Museum.

Kurseong's other life was religious and scholarly. From 1889 to 1971 St Mary's Hill held the Jesuit theological college that later moved to Delhi and became Vidyajyoti College of Theology. The town still has a dense ring of schools, from Dow Hill to St Alphonsus, and children in uniform are part of its morning traffic.

did_you_know: Sarat Chandra Bose bought the Giddapahar house in 1922; Subhas Chandra Bose was held under house arrest there in 1936, and it opened as a museum around 2000.
St Mary's Hill in Kurseong hosted a Jesuit theological college from 1889 to 1971; it then moved to Delhi as Vidyajyoti College of Theology.
Kurseong became a municipality in 1879 and the headquarters of a separate subdivision of Darjeeling district in 1890.
intro: Kurseong is the halfway town of the Darjeeling hills, and that is its strength. It is high enough to be cool and green, low enough to be mild in winter, and small enough to walk. The toy train shares Hill Cart Road with jeeps and shoppers in the bazaar, which makes for one of the oddest and most enjoyable railway sights in India. Around the town, tea slopes fall away on every side: Makaibari and Castleton to the south, Ambootia to the east, Goomtee and Jungpana further along.

Most visitors stop for tea and momos on the way to Darjeeling. We think it deserves two nights. Spend one morning at Netaji's house and Eagle's Crag, another walking up through the Dow Hill forest to the old schools and on to Chimney, and an afternoon down at Makaibari. Rooms cost less than in Darjeeling, food is cheap, and the town is quiet by 8 pm.

highlights.title: Netaji Museum at Giddapahar
highlights.text: The Bose family's hill house, where Subhas Chandra Bose was held under house arrest in 1936. Small rooms of photographs, letters and his furniture, and a view from the garden over the plains towards Siliguri. About 4 km from the bazaar.

highlights.title: Eagle's Crag
highlights.text: A viewpoint built around an old water reservoir on the hill above the town, with a small café and a deck looking over the tea gardens, the plains and, on clear winter mornings, the snow peaks to the north.

highlights.title: Toy train in the bazaar
highlights.text: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway runs down the middle of Kurseong's main street, and shopkeepers pull in their goods as the train edges past. Kurseong station has a small yard where you can watch locomotives being serviced.

highlights.title: Dow Hill and Chimney
highlights.text: A forest road climbs from town past Victoria Boys' School and Dow Hill School to the village of Chimney, named after the brick chimney of an old dak bungalow. A good half-day walk.

highlights.title: Makaibari tea estate
highlights.text: One of the oldest gardens in Darjeeling, with its factory first run in 1859. It lies on the Pankhabari road a short drive below the town; visit in the plucking season from March to November.

highlights.title: Cheap, filling food
highlights.text: Kurseong's bazaar is good for momos, thukpa, sel roti in festival season and plates of chowmein at ₹60–120. Tea shops near the station serve strong milk tea to the jeep drivers from early morning.

how_to_reach.text: From the Hill Cart Road stands near Siliguri Junction and the Tenzing Norgay bus terminus, jeeps leave when full from about 7 am, ₹150–200 a seat. Most take the faster Rohini road (about 1.5–2 hours); some use the old Hill Cart Road past Tindharia. From Darjeeling, jeeps cost ₹100–150 and take about 1.5 hours.

Kurseong is a station on the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway between NJP and Darjeeling. Services on the lower section have been interrupted for years at a time by landslides at Pagla Jhora and Tindharia, so book on IRCTC and check current status before you travel.

A car from NJP or Bagdogra costs about ₹2,000–2,800 depending on the vehicle and season. Ask the driver to use the Rohini road in daylight; it is shorter but very steep. From Darjeeling a car costs about ₹1,800–2,500.

where_to_stay: Stay on Hill Cart Road near the station if you want to walk to the bazaar and the toy train, or up towards Dow Hill for quiet and forest. The WBTDC Kurseong Tourist Lodge is the reliable government option, with the train passing its restaurant. For a single splurge night, Cochrane Place on the Pankhabari road is a heritage hotel with tea-garden views. On a budget, look at small family hotels around the station (₹1,200–2,200 a double) or go down to the Makaibari village homestays, which include dinner and breakfast.
tips: Visit Netaji's house in the morning and walk down via Eagle's Crag; check the museum's opening days first.
Take the Rohini road up in daylight only; it is short but has very tight hairpins.
Most shops in the bazaar close by 8 pm, so eat early.
Carry cash: card payments and ATMs are fine in town but rarer in the villages around.
Ask locally before walking through the Dow Hill forest late in the day; the road is lonely after dark.

experiences.title: Netaji's house at Giddapahar
experiences.cost: Free or a small fee · car ₹400–600 return from bazaar
experiences.image_query: Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose museum Kurseong
experiences.summary: Visit the hill house that Sarat Chandra Bose bought in 1922 and where his brother Subhas was held under house arrest in 1936. Small, quiet rooms of photographs and letters, and a garden that looks out over the plains.
body: Giddapahar is the hill rising above Kurseong to the south-west, about 4 km from the bazaar. The Bose house is a modest two-storey building in a garden of old trees. Sarat Chandra Bose, the lawyer and Congress leader, bought it in 1922 as a family retreat. His younger brother Subhas visited several times, and in 1936, after returning from Europe, the British held him here under house arrest for several months.

Inside, the rooms show family photographs, copies of letters and a few pieces of the family's furniture. During his confinement he wrote a number of political letters and letters to Emilie Schenkl, whom he later married. It is a small museum, so give it an hour and read the captions slowly. Opening days and hours change; check current status before you go.
Walk or drive back down via Eagle's Crag. The road gives long views over the plains towards Siliguri, best on a clear morning between October and March.

faqs.q: Why was Netaji held at Kurseong?
faqs.a: Subhas Chandra Bose returned to India from Europe in 1936 and was arrested. The British government then kept him under house arrest at his brother Sarat Chandra Bose's house at Giddapahar in Kurseong, away from political centres. He wrote many letters during that time, which the museum displays in copies.

faqs.q: How do I get to the Netaji Museum from Kurseong?
faqs.a: It is about 4 km uphill from the bazaar on the Giddapahar road. A local car costs about ₹400–600 return with waiting time. Fit walkers can go up in 1–1.5 hours and come down via Eagle's Crag. There is no regular shared jeep on this road.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at the Netaji Museum?
faqs.a: Entry has been free or a small fee in recent years. The museum closes on some days of the week and on certain holidays, and hours can change. Check current status before you travel, and avoid arriving in the lunch hour when staff may be away.

experiences.title: Morning at Eagle's Crag
experiences.summary: Climb to Kurseong's best town viewpoint, a deck built around the old water reservoir above the bazaar. On clear mornings you see the plains, the tea gardens and the snow peaks to the north.
body: Eagle's Crag is the high point just above Kurseong bazaar, a short, steep walk from the station area. The top is built around a water reservoir that supplies part of the town, with a viewing deck, benches, and a small café. Locals come up at dawn to walk, and on a clear day the view runs from the Siliguri plains and the Teesta and Mahananda river channels to the snows behind Darjeeling.

Go early. From October to March the mornings are usually clear until 9 or 10 am, after which haze rises from the plains. In the monsoon you will often stand inside a cloud. The climb takes 20–30 minutes from the bazaar.
Combine it with Netaji's house at Giddapahar on the same morning, or walk on towards Dow Hill if you want a longer day. Carry water; the café keeps irregular hours.

faqs.q: Can I see Kanchenjunga from Eagle's Crag?
faqs.a: On clear mornings from October to March you can see the snow peaks to the north, though Kanchenjunga is not as dominant as it is from Darjeeling. The best and most reliable view from the Crag is south over the plains and the tea gardens. Go before 8.30 am for the clearest air.

faqs.q: How long is the walk to Eagle's Crag?
faqs.a: About 20–30 minutes uphill from Kurseong bazaar or the station, on a steep lane and steps. It is fine for most walkers with a few stops. Taxis can drive most of the way if you have older people or small children with you.

faqs.q: Is Eagle's Crag worth visiting in the monsoon?
faqs.a: Only for the mood. From late June to September you will often see little more than cloud, and the steps can be slippery. In that season, visit a tea garden instead and come back to the Crag on a clear morning in October or November.

experiences.title: Toy train and bazaar walk
experiences.best_time: Late morning when a train is due, Oct–May
experiences.image_query: Darjeeling Himalayan Railway Kurseong station bazaar
experiences.summary: Walk Kurseong's Hill Cart Road from the station through the bazaar, timing it with a train. Watch the two-foot-gauge line squeeze between shops, and stop at the station yard to see the engines.
body: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway opened to Darjeeling in 1881 and was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999. In Kurseong it does something you rarely see anywhere: it runs straight down the main street. Shopkeepers move baskets and parked scooters, the driver sounds the horn every few metres, and the train crawls past the fronts of shops close enough to touch.

Start at Kurseong station, which has a small yard and sheds, and ask the staff when the next train is due. Then walk north through the bazaar towards the Tourist Lodge so that the train comes to you. Stop for tea at one of the stalls by the line.

Services change with the season and with landslide repairs on the lower line around Tindharia and Pagla Jhora. Check the current timetable on IRCTC or at the station, and do not walk on the track itself.

faqs.q: Which toy trains pass through Kurseong?
faqs.a: Kurseong lies on the NJP–Darjeeling line, and some services run only on the upper section between Kurseong and Darjeeling. The exact trains running vary with the season and with track repairs below Kurseong. Ask at the station or check IRCTC for the current timetable before planning your walk.

faqs.q: Can I ride the toy train from Kurseong to Darjeeling?
faqs.a: When services run, yes. The trip takes about 2.5–3 hours over 32 km and climbs through Tung, Sonada and Ghoom. Book on IRCTC; seats are limited. A shared jeep does the same trip in 1.5 hours for ₹100–150, so many travellers ride one way and jeep the other.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk along the line in the bazaar?
faqs.a: Walk on the road edge and the shop fronts, not on the track. The train moves slowly through town, but jeeps and scooters also use the road. Keep children close and step well back when you hear the horn.

experiences.title: Kurseong bazaar food crawl
experiences.summary: Eat your way down Hill Cart Road: steamed momos, thukpa, aloo dum, chowmein, and milk tea by the station. Cheap, filling, and a good way to meet the town as it finishes work.
body: Kurseong is a working town, and its food is built for students, drivers and office workers. Start near the station with a plate of steamed momos, pork, chicken or vegetable at ₹60–120. Follow it with aloo dum, potatoes in a spicy gravy that is a hill snack, or a bowl of thukpa if the evening is cold.

Look for seasonal things: sel roti, a ring-shaped rice bread, appears around Dashain and Tihar; churpi, dried yak or cow cheese, hangs at grocery counters; and fermented gundruk turns up in homestay soups in winter. Small bakeries sell cakes and biscuits that tea pickers buy for their children.
Finish with a glass of strong milk tea by the jeep stand. Most stalls close by 8 pm, and the town goes quiet soon after.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Kurseong?
faqs.a: Start with steamed momos and aloo dum, then try thukpa on a cold evening. Around Dashain and Tihar look for sel roti, the ring-shaped rice bread. Churpi, a hard dried cheese, is sold at grocery counters and makes a good trail snack. Most plates cost ₹60–150.

faqs.q: Is street food in Kurseong safe?
faqs.a: Eat where food is cooked fresh and turnover is high, which in Kurseong usually means the busy stalls near the station and the bazaar. Drink bottled or filtered water. Steamed momos straight from the steamer are a safe bet; skip anything left standing for hours.

faqs.q: Are there vegetarian options in Kurseong?
faqs.a: Yes. Vegetable momos, aloo dum, chowmein, thukpa without meat and simple dal-rice meals are easy to find. Small Bengali and Marwari eateries near the bazaar serve full vegetarian thalis for about ₹100–180. Homestays will cook vegetarian food if you tell them in advance.

faqs.q: Is Kurseong worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, especially if you prefer a working town to a tourist resort. In two days you can see Netaji's house, Eagle's Crag, the toy train in the bazaar, the Dow Hill forest and Makaibari's tea garden. It is cheaper and quieter than Darjeeling, and a good base for village day trips to Sittong and Chimney.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Kurseong?
faqs.a: Two nights is ideal. Day one covers Netaji's house, Eagle's Crag and the bazaar. Day two is a walk through Dow Hill to Chimney or a morning at Makaibari. Add a third night if you want a day trip to Sittong or Latpanchar, about an hour or more by car.

faqs.q: What does the name Kurseong mean?
faqs.a: The usual explanation is that it comes from the Lepcha word Kharsang, translated as 'land of the white orchid', after the white Coelogyne cristata orchid of these slopes. Some sources give 'small orchid', and another explanation links the name to a local cane. All three point to Lepcha roots older than the British town.

faqs.q: How far is Kurseong from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: About 32 km by Hill Cart Road. A shared jeep takes about 1.5 hours and costs ₹100–150 a seat; a reserved car costs about ₹1,800–2,500. The toy train, when running, takes 2.5–3 hours and climbs through Tung, Sonada and Ghoom on the way.

faqs.q: Is Kurseong colder than Darjeeling?
faqs.a: No, it is milder. At about 1,480 m Kurseong sits roughly 600 m below Darjeeling, so it is usually a few degrees warmer. Winter nights in December and January fall to around 5 °C, so you still need a jacket, but snow is very rare.

faqs.q: Where is the Netaji museum in Kurseong?
faqs.a: At Giddapahar, about 4 km uphill from the bazaar. It is in the house Sarat Chandra Bose bought in 1922, where Subhas Chandra Bose was held under house arrest in 1936. Hire a local car for ₹400–600 return or walk up in about an hour. Check opening days before you go.

faqs.q: Are there good budget hotels in Kurseong?
faqs.a: Yes. Small family-run hotels around the station and on Hill Cart Road charge ₹1,200–2,200 for a double room, less in winter and the monsoon. The government-run WBTDC Tourist Lodge is a step up. For meals included, the Makaibari village homestays below town cost about ₹1,500–2,000 per person.

faqs.q: Is Kurseong safe for solo travellers?
faqs.a: Kurseong is a calm, school-heavy town and solo travellers, including women, generally find it easy. Shared jeeps are the normal way to move around. Use ordinary care after dark, when the town goes quiet early, and avoid walking alone on forest roads such as Dow Hill late in the evening.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kurseong?
faqs.a: October to December for clear views and dry walking, with November the quietest. March to May is good for tea and flowers, with first flush in the gardens. July and August bring heavy rain and frequent landslides on the roads up from Siliguri, so avoid them unless you want a slow, rainy stay.
